title: Sliding-window SLA margin exploration
content:
Purpose: quick experiment notebook to understand how varying the sliding-window aggregation (window size + hop) for latency SLO calculation affects alerting sensitivity and inferred SLA margin. I want a pragmatic rule-of-thumb for what window/hop combos hide microbursts vs expose meaningful regressions when serving mixed-sequence-length traffic.

Background/context:
- Problem: Ops sees frequent transient SLO alerts that look noisy on the dashboards; engineering suspects alerting window config (sliding window 1m/5m etc) is masking or amplifying certain patterns.
- Goal: characterize false-positive alert rate vs detection latency for a set of synthetic traffic patterns.
- Constraints: keep experiments runnable on dev cluster (2x T4s), use existing load-generator harness (bench-gen v0.9), and the same model (gpt-small-v2 quantized) to avoid model-induced variance.

Key knobs under test:
- Window size (W): 30s, 60s, 120s, 300s
- Hop/slide (H): 10s, 30s, 60s
- Aggregation function: p95, p99, mean (mean only for reference)
- Alert threshold: SLO target 200ms p95; alert when windowed p95 > 200ms + margin (margin = 20ms, 50ms, 100ms)

Traffic patterns (each run = 30m):
1) Steady: constant qps=150, seq_len distribution: 50% 128, 50% 512 tokens
2) Microbursts: baseline qps=120, every 2m a 15s burst to qps=900 (short spikes)
3) Slow ramp: qps linearly increases from 100 to 400 over 30m
4) Sustained step: baseline 150 qps, at t=10m step up to 600 qps for 5m then back

Instrumentation/measurement:
- Collect per-request latency and timestamp; compute sliding-window aggregates offline to avoid runtime variability from metric pipeline.
- For each window config compute: number of alerts (windows where p95 > threshold), alert detection delay (time from start of real degradation to first alert), false positive windows during steady-state (windows flagged when no underlying long degradation present), and alert duration distribution.
- Also compute smoothed curves for visualization (EMA 30s) to compare human-observed vs alert-driven views.

Run summary (raw):
- Steady: W=30,H=10, p95 triggers often for margin=20ms (avg 3 FP per 30m), margin=50ms FP ~1, margin=100ms none. W=300,H=60 FP rare but missed short bursts.
- Microbursts: short 15s bursts are visible in W<=60 with H<=30 as spikes in p95 but only trigger alerts if margin small (20ms). With W=120,H=60 most microbursts are smoothed out and do not exceed threshold.
- Slow ramp: small windows (30s) produce many alerts during ramp; larger windows (300s) produce single alert but detection delay increases proportionally.
- Sustained step: all windows catch the step; detection delay ~~ W/2 on average, but W=30 catches faster.

Key observations (informal):
- Tradeoff is classic: smaller W catches fast regressions quickly but raises FP for minor jitter; larger W reduces noise but increases detection latency and tends to hide microbursts entirely.
- Hop size H matters for alert frequency granularity but has smaller impact than W. Using H ~= W/2 is a reasonable default to reduce redundant alerts while preserving detection speed.
- p99 is much noisier; for p99-based SLOs need larger W to avoid FP (but that hurts detection time). Consider hybrid: use p95 for alerting fast-sensitive, p99 for periodic analysis/rollups.

Quantitative notes (selected slices):
- Microbursts pattern, margin=50ms: W30/H10 -> alerts: 18 per 30m (many align with bursts); W120/H60 -> alerts: 3 per 30m (only the loudest clusters), detection delay median: 8s (W30) vs 60s (W120).
- Slow ramp, margin=20ms: W30 -> 12 alerts across ramp, W300 -> 1 alert starting ~7m into ramp (detection delay ~210s).

Practical recommendations for production (first pass):
- SLO p95 for most user-facing inference endpoints. Default sliding window: W=60s, H=30s with alert margin = 50ms for endpoints with 50-200ms baseline latency.
- For endpoints with baseline <50ms set margin smaller (20ms) but increase W to 120s to avoid noise from infra jitter.
- For critical low-latency SLAs where microbursts matter (audio real-time, interactive experiences), use paired alerts: fast window (W=30/H=10, margin small) to notify ops but mark those as "informational" unless sustained across a larger window (W=120) to reduce toil.
- p99 should be monitored but not primary alerting signal unless traffic volume supports stable p99 estimates; use p99 for weekly/per-deploy health checks.

Open questions / next experiments:
- How do request size / seq_len mixes interact with windowing? I suspect heavy tails from long sequences inflate p95 spikes; need runs where burst is from long sequences rather than QPS.
- Can we tune adaptive windows: e.g., auto-expand W during noisy intervals and shrink when stable? Prototype idea: if a short-window spike is observed, require confirmation in the next W_long before firing a page.
- Explore combining rate-of-change heuristics (delta-over-baseline) to reduce FP for microbursts that return to baseline quickly.

Immediate TODOs:
- Run variant where microbursts are caused by 10x longer sequences instead of QPS spike (assigned to Nora)
- Add dashboard mock that shows paired-alert logic (fast/informational + sustained/actionable) (assigned to Liam)
- Share short note with SRE and rotations and propose default W=60/H=30 + suggested margins (small RFC).

Appendix: quick ASCII timeline (microburst run, W=60/H=30):
- 00:00 baseline 120 qps
- 02:00 burst 15s -> p95 jump to 420ms -> alert window starting 02:00 (alerts count 1)
- 04:00 baseline
- Repeats every 2m; with W=60/H=30 we saw alerts for ~70% of bursts (others diluted by window overlap)

Notes to self: consolidate these runs into bench-gen config files, attach raw CSVs to GH run. Keep margins conservative for now to avoid waking on-call for harmless microbursts. Consider adding jitter budget to SLO page so product owners understand tradeoffs.
